courses.title: Chemotherapy: Antimicrobials, Antimalarials, Antiretrovirals and Anticancer Drugs
courses.description: Principles of antimicrobial therapy, major antibacterial classes, anti-TB drugs, antimalarials, antiretrovirals and antifungals, anthelmintics and cancer chemotherapy.

topics.title: Principles of Antimicrobial Therapy and Stewardship
topics.summary: Bactericidal vs bacteriostatic, spectrum, choice of drug, combination therapy and stewardship.

material.heading: Principles
material.body: Selective toxicity is the basis of antimicrobial therapy. Bactericidal drugs kill bacteria (β-lactams, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, metronidazole, vancomycin); bacteriostatic drugs inhibit growth (tetracyclines, macrolides, sulphonamides, chloramphenicol, clindamycin). Choice depends on the likely organism (empirical therapy guided by local antibiograms), site of infection and drug penetration (e.g. CSF — ceftriaxone), patient factors (allergy, age, pregnancy, renal and hepatic function), and cost. Time-dependent killing (β-lactams — keep concentrations above MIC) versus concentration-dependent killing (aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones — high peaks; once-daily aminoglycosides). Combination therapy prevents resistance (TB, HIV) or broadens cover.

material.heading: Stewardship
material.body: Antimicrobial resistance is a major threat, worsened in Nigeria by self-medication, over-the-counter antibiotic sales, poor-quality and falsified medicines, incomplete courses and agricultural use. Antimicrobial stewardship promotes the right drug, right dose, right route and right duration; taking cultures before starting antibiotics; de-escalating to narrower agents when results return; switching IV to oral when appropriate; and not treating viral infections (e.g. common colds) with antibiotics. WHO's AWaRe classification groups antibiotics into Access (first-choice, e.g. amoxicillin), Watch (higher resistance potential, e.g. ceftriaxone, ciprofloxacin, azithromycin) and Reserve (last resort, e.g. colistin, linezolid) categories. Nigeria has a National Action Plan on AMR (One Health approach).

questions.stem: Which antibiotic is bacteriostatic?
questions.explanation: Tetracyclines inhibit protein synthesis without killing.

questions.stem: β-lactam antibiotics show killing that is mainly:
questions.explanation: Efficacy depends on time above MIC.

questions.stem: Aminoglycosides are often given once daily because their killing is:
questions.explanation: High peaks maximise killing and reduce toxicity.

questions.stem: In the WHO AWaRe classification, amoxicillin is in the:
questions.explanation: Access antibiotics are first-choice for common infections.

questions.stem: Ceftriaxone and ciprofloxacin are classified by WHO AWaRe as:

questions.stem: An antimicrobial stewardship principle is to:
options: Use the broadest drug for every infection

questions.explanation: Targeted therapy reduces resistance.

questions.stem: Which practice drives antimicrobial resistance in Nigeria?
questions.explanation: Unregulated access encourages misuse.

questions.stem: Combination therapy is used in TB and HIV mainly to:
questions.explanation: Multiple drugs make resistance much less likely.

topics.title: Major Antibacterial Classes
topics.summary: Mechanisms, uses and adverse effects of penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, aminoglycosides, quinolones and others.

material.heading: Cell-wall and protein synthesis inhibitors
material.body: Penicillins (benzylpenicillin, amoxicillin, co-amoxiclav, flucloxacillin, piperacillin–tazobactam) inhibit cell-wall cross-linking; main adverse effect is hypersensitivity (rash to anaphylaxis; about 10% cross-reactivity with cephalosporins historically cited, now thought lower). Cephalosporins: first generation (cefalexin — skin), third generation (ceftriaxone — meningitis, gonorrhoea, typhoid, severe pneumonia; ceftazidime — Pseudomonas). Carbapenems (meropenem) — reserved for resistant organisms. Vancomycin (glycopeptide) — MRSA and C. difficile (oral); nephrotoxic and 'red man syndrome' with rapid infusion. Aminoglycosides (gentamicin, amikacin) — Gram-negative sepsis; nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity (monitor levels). Macrolides (erythromycin, azithromycin, clarithromycin) — atypical pneumonia, chlamydia; QT prolongation, CYP3A4 inhibition (erythromycin, clarithromycin). Tetracyclines (doxycycline) — chlamydia, rickettsia, acne, malaria prophylaxis; avoid in pregnancy and under 8 years.
keyPoints: Doxycycline: avoid in pregnancy and < 8 years

material.heading: Other antibacterials
material.body: Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) inhibit DNA gyrase — UTIs, typhoid (where susceptible), Gram-negative infections; adverse effects: tendinopathy and tendon rupture, QT prolongation, seizures, cartilage concerns in children. Co-trimoxazole (trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole) — UTIs, Pneumocystis pneumonia prophylaxis and treatment in HIV; rash, Stevens–Johnson syndrome, bone marrow suppression, hyperkalaemia. Metronidazole — anaerobes and protozoa (amoebiasis, giardiasis, trichomoniasis, bacterial vaginosis, C. difficile); disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol, metallic taste. Nitrofurantoin — uncomplicated lower UTI (avoid in renal impairment and at term). Chloramphenicol — broad spectrum; grey baby syndrome in neonates and aplastic anaemia. Clindamycin — anaerobes, bone infections; C. difficile colitis risk.

questions.stem: The most common serious adverse effect of penicillins is:
questions.explanation: Allergy ranges from rash to anaphylaxis.

questions.stem: The antibiotic of choice for empirical treatment of bacterial meningitis in Nigeria is:
questions.explanation: Ceftriaxone penetrates CSF and covers common pathogens.

questions.stem: Gentamicin requires monitoring because of:
questions.explanation: Aminoglycosides damage kidneys and the inner ear.

questions.stem: Tendon rupture is a recognised adverse effect of:
questions.explanation: Fluoroquinolones cause tendinopathy, especially the Achilles.

questions.stem: Patients taking metronidazole should avoid alcohol because of:
questions.explanation: It causes flushing, vomiting and palpitations.

questions.stem: Grey baby syndrome in neonates is caused by:
questions.explanation: Neonates cannot glucuronidate chloramphenicol.

questions.stem: Prophylaxis against Pneumocystis pneumonia in HIV uses:
questions.explanation: Cotrimoxazole also reduces other infections.

questions.stem: 'Red man syndrome' is associated with rapid infusion of:
questions.explanation: Histamine release causes flushing; slow the infusion.

topics.title: Anti-TB Drugs, Antimalarials and Antiretrovirals
topics.summary: First-line TB drugs and their toxicities, antimalarial drugs, and ARV classes.

material.heading: Anti-TB drugs
material.body: First-line: rifampicin (orange-red body fluids, hepatotoxicity, potent enzyme inducer — reduces efficacy of oral contraceptives, some ARVs, warfarin), isoniazid (peripheral neuropathy — prevent with pyridoxine; hepatotoxicity), pyrazinamide (hepatotoxicity, hyperuricaemia/gout) and ethambutol (optic neuritis — reduced visual acuity and red–green colour vision; check vision). Drug-induced hepatitis is the most important shared toxicity. Streptomycin (injectable, ototoxic) is now rarely used first-line. Drug-resistant TB uses newer regimens (bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid, moxifloxacin — BPaLM). Isoniazid preventive therapy (or 3HP) is given to eligible people with HIV and child contacts.

material.heading: Antimalarials and antiretrovirals
material.body: Antimalarials: artemisinin derivatives (artesunate, artemether — rapid parasite clearance), partner drugs (lumefantrine, amodiaquine, piperaquine, mefloquine), quinine (cinchonism — tinnitus, headache; hypoglycaemia), sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine (IPTp; avoid with cotrimoxazole), primaquine (radical cure; haemolysis in G6PD deficiency), proguanil (prophylaxis in sickle cell disease). Antiretroviral classes: NRTIs (tenofovir — renal toxicity and bone loss; lamivudine; abacavir — hypersensitivity with HLA-B*5701; zidovudine — anaemia), NNRTIs (efavirenz — vivid dreams, dizziness; nevirapine — rash, hepatotoxicity), integrase inhibitors (dolutegravir — preferred first-line; weight gain; interaction with polyvalent cations — separate from antacids and iron), protease inhibitors (lopinavir/ritonavir, atazanavir/ritonavir — metabolic effects, CYP3A4 interactions). Post-exposure prophylaxis (within 72 hours, for 28 days) and pre-exposure prophylaxis (tenofovir-based) prevent HIV.

questions.stem: Orange-red discolouration of urine and tears is caused by:
questions.explanation: Rifampicin colours body fluids harmlessly.

questions.stem: Pyridoxine is given with isoniazid to prevent:
questions.explanation: Isoniazid antagonises vitamin B6.

questions.stem: Visual acuity and colour vision should be monitored in patients taking:
questions.explanation: Ethambutol causes optic neuritis.

questions.stem: Hyperuricaemia and gout are associated with:
questions.explanation: Pyrazinamide reduces urate excretion.

questions.stem: Tinnitus, headache and hypoglycaemia during malaria treatment suggest toxicity from:
questions.explanation: Cinchonism and hypoglycaemia are quinine effects.

questions.stem: Tenofovir requires monitoring of:
questions.explanation: It can cause proximal tubular injury.

questions.stem: Dolutegravir absorption is reduced if taken at the same time as:
questions.explanation: Polyvalent cations chelate integrase inhibitors.

questions.stem: HIV post-exposure prophylaxis should be started within:
questions.explanation: Earlier is better; the course lasts 28 days.

topics.title: Antifungals and Anthelmintics
topics.summary: Azoles, polyenes and echinocandins; anthelmintic drugs and mass drug administration.

material.heading: Antifungals
material.body: Polyenes bind ergosterol, forming membrane pores: amphotericin B (IV — severe systemic infections such as cryptococcal meningitis; nephrotoxicity, hypokalaemia, infusion reactions; liposomal forms less toxic) and nystatin (topical/oral suspension for oral thrush — not absorbed). Azoles inhibit ergosterol synthesis (lanosterol 14α-demethylase): fluconazole (candidiasis, cryptococcal maintenance), itraconazole (histoplasmosis), voriconazole (aspergillosis), ketoconazole/clotrimazole/miconazole (topical) — azoles inhibit CYP450, causing drug interactions. Echinocandins (caspofungin) inhibit cell-wall β-glucan synthesis. Flucytosine is combined with amphotericin in cryptococcal meningitis. Griseofulvin and terbinafine treat dermatophyte infections of hair and nails (tinea capitis — griseofulvin with fatty food; terbinafine).
keyPoints: Azoles inhibit ergosterol synthesis and CYP450

material.heading: Anthelmintics
material.body: Albendazole and mebendazole (benzimidazoles, inhibit microtubule formation) treat soil-transmitted helminths (Ascaris, hookworm, Trichuris) and are used in school deworming; avoid in the first trimester. Praziquantel (increases calcium permeability, paralysing worms) treats schistosomiasis and tapeworms (including neurocysticercosis with albendazole and steroids). Ivermectin (glutamate-gated chloride channels) treats onchocerciasis, strongyloidiasis and scabies; mass drug administration uses ivermectin with albendazole for lymphatic filariasis and onchocerciasis (caution where Loa loa is co-endemic — risk of encephalopathy). Diethylcarbamazine (DEC) for filariasis is avoided in onchocerciasis (Mazzotti reaction). Pyrantel pamoate is safe in pregnancy for roundworm and pinworm.

questions.stem: Oral thrush in an infant is commonly treated with:
questions.explanation: Nystatin acts locally without systemic absorption.

questions.stem: A major toxicity of amphotericin B is:
questions.explanation: It damages renal tubules.

questions.stem: Azole antifungals act by:
questions.explanation: They inhibit lanosterol 14α-demethylase.

questions.stem: Tinea capitis in children is treated with:
questions.explanation: Hair infections need systemic therapy.

questions.stem: School deworming programmes in Nigeria use:
questions.explanation: Benzimidazoles treat soil-transmitted helminths.

questions.stem: The drug of choice for schistosomiasis is:
questions.explanation: Praziquantel is effective against all schistosome species.

questions.stem: Ivermectin mass treatment must be used cautiously where which parasite is co-endemic?
questions.explanation: High Loa loa loads risk severe encephalopathy.

questions.stem: Ivermectin is effective against:
questions.explanation: It kills microfilariae and mites.

topics.title: Cancer Chemotherapy
topics.summary: Cell cycle and drug classes, common toxicities and their management, and targeted and hormonal therapies.

material.heading: Drug classes
material.body: Cytotoxic drugs target rapidly dividing cells. Classes: alkylating agents (cyclophosphamide — haemorrhagic cystitis prevented with mesna; chlorambucil), platinum compounds (cisplatin — nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, severe emesis), antimetabolites (methotrexate — folate antagonist, rescued with folinic acid/leucovorin; 5-fluorouracil; capecitabine; cytarabine; 6-mercaptopurine — interacts with allopurinol), anthracyclines (doxorubicin — cumulative cardiotoxicity; red urine), vinca alkaloids (vincristine — peripheral neuropathy, fatal if given intrathecally; vinblastine — myelosuppression), taxanes (paclitaxel, docetaxel — neuropathy, hypersensitivity), bleomycin (pulmonary fibrosis), etoposide (topoisomerase II inhibitor). Combination regimens use drugs with different mechanisms and toxicities (e.g. CHOP for lymphoma; ABVD for Hodgkin).

material.heading: Toxicities and targeted therapy
material.body: Common toxicities: myelosuppression (neutropenic sepsis is an emergency — broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour), nausea and vomiting (ondansetron, dexamethasone, aprepitant), mucositis, alopecia, infertility, tumour lysis syndrome (hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, hyperuricaemia, hypocalcaemia and AKI — prevent with hydration and allopurinol or rasburicase, e.g. in Burkitt lymphoma), and extravasation injury. Safe handling of cytotoxics protects staff. Targeted therapies: imatinib (BCR-ABL in CML), trastuzumab (HER2-positive breast cancer — cardiotoxicity), rituximab (anti-CD20 in B-cell lymphomas). Hormonal therapy: tamoxifen (oestrogen receptor modulator — risk of endometrial cancer and thromboembolism) and aromatase inhibitors (letrozole, anastrozole — postmenopausal ER-positive breast cancer) and androgen deprivation for prostate cancer.
keyPoints: Tamoxifen: endometrial cancer and VTE risk

questions.stem: Mesna is given with cyclophosphamide to prevent:
questions.explanation: Mesna neutralises the toxic metabolite acrolein in the bladder.

questions.stem: Folinic acid (leucovorin) is used to rescue patients from toxicity of:
questions.explanation: It bypasses the DHFR block.

questions.stem: Cumulative cardiotoxicity is characteristic of:
questions.explanation: Anthracyclines damage the myocardium in a dose-dependent way.

questions.stem: Vincristine must never be given by which route because it is fatal?
questions.explanation: Intrathecal vincristine causes fatal neurotoxicity.

questions.stem: Pulmonary fibrosis is a well-known toxicity of:
questions.explanation: Bleomycin causes dose-related lung damage.

questions.stem: A febrile patient with neutropenia after chemotherapy should receive:
options: Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within one hour
questions.explanation: Neutropenic sepsis is rapidly fatal if untreated.

questions.stem: Tumour lysis syndrome is prevented by hydration and:
questions.explanation: These reduce uric acid formation.

questions.stem: Trastuzumab targets:
questions.explanation: It is used for HER2-positive breast cancer.
